howItWorks.intro: The calculator grosses up your target take-home income to cover business expenses, then divides that grossed-up number by the billable hours you can realistically sell in a year — not the total hours you work. That distinction is the whole point of pricing by the hour: a 40-hour work week rarely converts into 40 billable hours, and treating it as if it does is the single most common reason freelance hourly rates come in too low.

rules.name: Hourly Rate
rules.explanation: Target income grossed up for expenses divided by billable hours.

howItWorks.outro: This math tells you the floor, not the market rate. Once you know the minimum you need per hour to hit your income goal, check it against what comparable freelancers in your field actually charge — if the market rate sits well above your floor, price closer to the market; if it sits below, you have a hard decision to make about hours, expenses, or income targets before you take on more clients at a rate that quietly loses money.

faq.question: Why does my freelance hourly rate need to be so much higher than my old salary divided by 2,080 hours?
faq.answer: Because that division assumes every one of those 2,080 hours is billable and that your employer isn't paying for anything beyond your paycheck. Neither is true once you freelance. You lose paid time off, employer-covered health insurance, retirement matching, and payroll taxes your employer used to split with you — and you gain hours spent on invoicing, proposals, admin, and finding the next client, none of which a client pays for directly. A rate built on 2,080 hours and no expense buffer is usually 40-50% too low.

faq.question: What counts as a billable hour versus a working hour?
faq.answer: A billable hour is time a client actually pays for — the work itself. A working hour includes everything else it takes to run a freelance business: sending invoices, chasing late payments, writing proposals, updating your portfolio, bookkeeping, client calls that aren't scoped into a project, and slow stretches between gigs. Most established freelancers bill 50-70% of a 40-hour week, which works out to roughly 20-28 billable hours. New freelancers often bill closer to the low end while they're still building a client base.

faq.question: How does self-employment tax change the math?
faq.answer: As a W-2 employee, you pay 7.65% of your wages toward Social Security and Medicare, and your employer quietly pays the other 7.65% on your behalf. As a freelancer, you're both the employee and the employer, so you owe the full 15.3% yourself — roughly double what came out of your old paycheck. That's on top of ordinary income tax. Building a 20-30% overhead buffer into your income target, rather than treating self-employment tax as an afterthought, is how you avoid a surprise bill in April.

faq.question: What's a realistic billable-hours target if I'm just starting out?
faq.answer: Plan for 40-50% utilization in your first six to twelve months rather than the 60-70% an established freelancer might hit — you'll be spending disproportionate time on marketing, pricing experiments, and building the systems (contracts, invoicing, a portfolio) that later free up billable hours. Entering a lower billable-hours figure into the calculator now gives you an honest rate instead of one that assumes a client roster you haven't built yet.

faq.question: Should I quote clients an hourly rate, a day rate, or a project price?
faq.answer: This calculator is built around the hourly figure because it's the cleanest way to check that any pricing structure actually clears your floor. Once you have your minimum hourly rate, the day rate shown alongside it (8 billable hours) works for clients who prefer a daily figure, and you can convert to a flat project price by estimating hours and multiplying — just make sure your hour estimate is honest about scope creep, revisions, and the non-billable coordination a project inevitably includes.

faq.question: How often should I revisit my hourly rate?
faq.answer: Recalculate at least once a year, and any time one of the four inputs meaningfully shifts — a jump in health insurance premiums, a change in how many weeks off you're taking, a client base that's finally letting you push utilization higher, or a year where your actual expense percentage came in higher than you estimated. Freelancers who set a rate once and never revisit it tend to fall behind inflation and rising overhead within two or three years.

howWeCalculate.intro: The calculator takes your target take-home income and grosses it up for business expenses before dividing by billable hours, so the expense percentage and the hours figure both pull real weight in the final number — not just the income target.
steps: Start from your target annual income — the take-home number you actually want to clear after business costs, before income tax
Divide your weekly billable hours by 40 to get a utilization rate, then multiply by your working weeks (52 minus weeks off) to find total billable hours for the year
Gross up the income target by your business expense percentage, which should include software, insurance, equipment, and a buffer for self-employment tax
Divide the grossed-up income by total annual billable hours to get your minimum hourly rate, then derive the day rate (8 billable hours) and weekly rate from that same number
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This is a pricing floor built from your own inputs, not tax or legal advice. Self-employment tax rules, deductible expenses, and health insurance costs vary by location and business structure — confirm the specifics with an accountant before you finalize a rate you'll quote to clients.

whenToUse.intro: This calculator is built for the specific moment of setting or resetting an hourly number — not for pricing a one-off project or negotiating a day rate, though the results feed into both.
scenarios: You're leaving a salaried job for freelance work and need a starting rate that replaces your old take-home pay once benefits, taxes, and non-billable hours are accounted for
A client asks 'what's your rate?' and you want a defensible floor rather than a number pulled from what a friend charges
Your billable hours dropped last quarter and you're deciding whether to raise your rate or take on more clients to hit the same income target
You're comparing an hourly arrangement against a flat project quote and want to check that the implied hourly rate on the project actually clears your minimum
Your business expenses changed — new software subscriptions, higher insurance premiums, a coworking membership — and you need to see how that shifts the rate you should be charging
You're reviewing rates annually and want to sanity-check whether last year's number still covers this year's costs and income goal

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Solves
sections.body: Most freelancers set an hourly rate by guessing, copying what a competitor charges, or taking their old salary and dividing by 2,080 hours. This calculator works backward from what you actually need to earn. Enter your target annual take-home income, the hours per week you expect to spend on billable client work — not total working hours — how many weeks you'll take off, and the share of revenue that goes to business expenses. The result is a floor: the minimum hourly rate that covers your income goal, your costs, and the hours you can realistically sell, shown as an hourly rate alongside the equivalent day rate (8 billable hours) and weekly rate so you can quote whichever unit a client asks for.

sections.title: Why a Freelance Hourly Rate Runs Higher Than a Salaried Equivalent
sections.body: A salaried employee's rough hourly equivalent — annual pay divided by 2,080 hours — undercounts everything freelancing removes: employer-paid health insurance, retirement matching, paid time off, and half of Social Security and Medicare taxes. Self-employed workers owe the full 15.3% self-employment tax rather than the roughly 7.65% withheld from a W-2 paycheck, because there's no employer to split it with. Consider someone targeting $80,000 in annual take-home pay who can bill 25 hours a week — 65% utilization on a 40-hour week — across 48 working weeks: that's 1,200 billable hours a year. Add roughly 20% for overhead — software, insurance, and a self-employment tax buffer — and the income target becomes $96,000. $96,000 ÷ 1,200 hours = $80/hour, noticeably higher than the naive $80,000 ÷ 2,000 hours = $40/hour a salaried-style calculation would suggest. Charging $40/hour under those same conditions leaves roughly $48,000 in take-home pay, not $80,000.

sections.title: The Billable-Hours Gap Is Where New Freelancers Underprice
sections.body: The 65% utilization in that example isn't a worst case — it's close to typical. Most freelancers bill somewhere between 50% and 70% of a 40-hour week once invoicing, proposals, client calls that fall outside a scoped project, bookkeeping, and slow stretches between contracts are accounted for. Someone who assumes 40 billable hours a week and prices accordingly is quietly working for less than they think, because the other 12-20 hours of running a business still have to get paid for out of the same revenue. Entering an honest billable-hours figure — not an aspirational one — is what keeps this calculator's output from being an underestimate.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Target Annual Income
howToSteps.description: Enter the take-home pay you want to clear in a year, before income tax. This is the number you're solving for, so start with a figure you can defend — what covers your living costs plus savings, not a number pulled out of thin air.

howToSteps.title: Set Your Billable Hours per Week
howToSteps.description: Enter the hours per week you expect to spend on paid client work, not the hours you're at your desk. If you're not sure, use 50-65% of a 40-hour week as a starting estimate — lower if you're new to freelancing, higher if you have a steady client base and lean systems for admin.

howToSteps.title: Add Weeks Off and Business Expenses
howToSteps.description: Weeks off should include vacation, sick time, and any slow periods you expect between contracts. Business expenses should cover software, insurance, equipment, professional fees, and a buffer for self-employment tax — 20-30% is a reasonable starting range for most solo freelancers.

howToSteps.title: Calculate and Compare Against the Market
howToSteps.description: Click Calculate to see your minimum hourly rate, day rate, and weekly rate. Treat the hourly figure as a floor, then check it against what comparable freelancers in your field charge — if the market rate is higher, price closer to the market rather than settling for your bare minimum.

tips: Enter your real billable-hours expectation, not an aspirational one — if you're not tracking your time yet, assume 50-60% utilization for your first year and adjust once you have data.

Build a self-employment tax buffer into your expense percentage rather than treating it as a separate line item you'll deal with later; 15.3% on top of income tax adds up fast if it isn't priced in from the start.
Recalculate whenever a fixed cost changes — a health insurance premium increase or a new required subscription should move your rate, not just your budget.

Compare the day rate this calculator produces against day-rate quotes you receive from clients directly — if a client's day-rate offer implies an hourly figure below your floor, it's underpriced even if the total sounds reasonable.
If your calculated rate feels too high to quote confidently, the fix is usually raising utilization or trimming expenses, not lowering your income target and quietly accepting less.
